newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat, Mubarak discuss Mideast peace crisis.
newsitem.headline: Arafat, Mubarak discuss Mideast peace crisis.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Thursday Egypt was unconvinced by new proposals on the troubled Middle East peace process brought to Cairo by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's envoy.

He was speaking after senior Egyptian officials briefed Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on talks between Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser Dore Gold and Mubarak's senior political adviser Osama el-Baz.
Mubarak and Arafat discussed for almost three hours the crisis in the Middle East peace talks sparked by Israel's decision to start building a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Gold told reporters before meeting Baz: "I'm here to convey a message from Israel to Egypt and we have a very new proposal about the peace process to discuss."

He was apparently referring to Netanyahu's offer to complete the "final status" talks within six months, nearly two years earlier than planned. Palestinian officials have dismissed the proposal as a trick.

"His (Gold's) proposals are unconvincing," Moussa told Reuters. "I am unable now to say what these proposals are but I would like to tell you all that any ideas they are talking about that try to justify or circumvent what's happening in Jerusalem is rejected."
Moussa said Arafat, who did not speak to reporters, was "frustrated" but had not given up on peace.
"The man is frustrated but he is still the leader of the Palestinians and Chairman Arafat and President Mubarak and all of us are committed to the peace process," Moussa said.

"The position of Mr. Arafat is known and it is based on the fact that the Palestinians will not accept any meddling with Jerusalem. The Palestinian position is very clear that any demographic, geographic or legal change in Jerusalem is totally rejected by Arabs and the international community. This position is unequivocal," he added.

Arab officials say the Oslo agreement between Israel and the Palestinians says the status of Jerusalem was for negotiation and that no one should take unilateral measures there -- an argument that the Israeli government rejects.

Israel considers Jerusalem -- the Arab eastern half of which it occupied in the 1967 Middle East war -- to be its undivided capital. But Palestinians view the eastern part as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Cairo on Thursday was at the hub of Arab diplomatic meetings on the latest crisis in the peace process.

Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara and Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, who both met Mubarak separately earlier, said Israel was killing the peace process, especially by starting to build more Jewish housing in Jebel Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa.
